::: {.hero-bio}
Nitish Nigam is an Assistant Professor of Economics at the Chandragupt Institute of Management Patna. His research lies at the intersection of behavioural economics, environmental economics and public policy, with a focus on sustainability transitions, technology adoption and climate resilience in emerging economies. Drawing on causal inference, discrete choice experiments and large-scale primary surveys, he examines how households and farmers respond to new technologies and public programmes, and what those responses imply for the design of policy.

His work has appeared in the *Journal of Environmental Management* and the *International Journal of Social Economics*. He is Project Director of an ICSSR-funded study on the adoption of climate-smart agriculture, and Co-Principal Investigator on studies of urban biodiversity governance and biological resource value chains for the Bihar State Biodiversity Board. Before joining the CIMP faculty, he served as a Research Associate with the State Transformation Cell of the State Support Mission (NITI Aayog) in Patna.

He holds a doctorate (FPM) in Economics from CIMP, an MA in Economics from the Central University of South Bihar and a BA (Hons) in Economics from Patna University. At CIMP he teaches Business Economics and Business Marketing, and he regularly leads executive education and faculty development programmes on causal inference, choice experiments, survey design and applied research methods.
:::

## What I work on

::: {.theme}
### Energy transition
Why Indian households buy electric vehicles or hold back, and which state policies change that, studied through choice experiments with consumers in Bihar and analysis across Indian states.
:::

::: {.theme}
### Climate-resilient agriculture
Which climate-smart practices farmers adopt and why, and which interventions farmers in Bihar's aspirational blocks actually prefer.
:::

::: {.theme}
### Biodiversity and natural resources
How Bihar governs its urban biodiversity, and how biological resources are harvested, traded and given value, in studies for the Bihar State Biodiversity Board.
:::

::: {.theme}
### Public programmes
Whether institutions make agricultural schemes work for beneficiary households, and whether female supervision raises women's participation in public employment programmes.
:::
